title: Samcrac's Back-Lot Aston Martin DBS: A V12 That Keeps Failing, and Signs of Tampering
dek: Samcrac bought a broken first-generation DBS V12 off a Florida dealer's back lot. So far he has found a fault that keeps coming back and, he says, signs that someone tampered with the car.

verdict: Too early to call. Samcrac hasn't said what he paid, and so far the titles describe an engine that "keeps failing" and possible tampering rather than a fix [2][3]. A sorted, clean-title first-generation DBS coupe sells for roughly $60,000 to $105,000 [4], so there's room to make money if the fault is ignition or wiring. If it's internal engine damage, the room disappears. His last DBS, a flood car, sold for $500 more than he paid [5]. This one starts with fewer unknowns, but the open question is the same: whether the V12 can be fixed cheaply.
body:
## The buy

Samcrac's newest Aston Martin came from the back lot of a Florida dealership, not from a salvage yard. His first video on it, posted on September 22, 2026, is titled "I Bought a Broken V12 Aston Martin from the Back Lot of a Florida Dealership" [1]. The title names the car only as a V12 DBS, and later titles call it a "$100k" or "$100,000" car [2][3]. The video descriptions we could read are sponsor messages. They give no price, model year, mileage or dealer name, and no outside outlet had reported on this car when we checked. So **we do not know what he paid**. The $100,000 figure reads like the car's market or advertised value, not his purchase price.

The $100,000 figure is also the best clue to which DBS this is. A 2019-on DBS Superleggera still sells for far more than that. The first-generation DBS V12, built from 2008 to 2012, sits right around it: CLASSIC.COM's benchmark for an automatic coupe is about $88,900, and manual coupes average about $144,000 [4]. We treat it as a 2008-2012 DBS V12. The exact year, body and gearbox are not confirmed, and the 2010 in this file is a placeholder for that range.

This is Samcrac's second DBS. In early 2025 he bought a flood-damaged DBS at a South Florida salvage auction for $28,000. He tried a $60 donor junction box from a Volvo, could not get the car running reliably, and sold it for $28,500 [5]. That history matters here. A dealer back-lot car usually arrives with fewer unknowns than a flood car, but it also reached the back lot for a reason.

## The damage

What we know comes from three video titles. The car was bought broken [1]. Six days later Samcrac was "looking inside" the V12 engine "to see why it keeps failing" [2], which points to a fault that keeps coming back rather than a single dead part. On October 18 he posted "Someone Tampered With My $100,000 Aston Martin DBS" [3]. The title does not say what was tampered with, who did it, or when. From titles alone we can't tell whether that happened before or after the sale. The descriptions add nothing, so we leave the diagnosis open.

## The work and the parts

None of the published descriptions list parts bought or prices paid, so the parts list in this file shows the usual suspects, marked as estimates. It is not a record of what Samcrac fitted. On the Aston V12, a fault that keeps coming back usually starts with ignition: twelve coil packs and twelve spark plugs. Eurospares lists the DBS plugs at £23.41 for a pack of four, so a set of twelve is about $93 at $1.33 to the pound [7]. It shows the coil pack's part number but no price. Owners also watch the catalytic converters, which can break up after misfires. A misfire fix that skips the cats risks bigger engine damage, which may be why he looked inside the engine. A long-parked car also usually needs a battery. If the tampering turns out to be wiring or ignition work, the bill could be small. If debris has reached the cylinders, it won't be.

## The money

With no stated purchase price and no parts receipts, the cost side is blank. The value side is clearer. On the CLASSIC.COM market page, recent automatic coupes sold for $88,600 on Bring a Trailer in September 2026, €89,000 (about $103,200 at $1.16 to the euro) on Collecting Cars in August, and $61,600 at Mecum Monterey in August [4]. A Hagerty past-sales record shows a 2010 DBS coupe sold for $123,045 [8], and dealers are asking about $89,700 to $102,400 for 2011-2012 automatics. Manual cars ask far more [4].

A dealer back-lot car most likely has a clean title, but no source confirms that. If the title is branded, expect it to be worth 20 to 40 percent less than a clean-title car [6]. A known engine history will also push buyers toward the low end. Fixed and sorted with a clean title, the car looks like a $55,000 to $95,000 automatic coupe. Unfixed, it's worth whatever the next person will pay to take the gamble.

## What's next

The next videos need to answer three questions. What was tampered with? Is the V12 itself healthy? And what did the car cost him? If the engine is sound and the fault turns out to be ignition or wiring, the car could be a cheap way into a V12 Aston. If the engine needs to come apart, the bill climbs fast. His last DBS showed how easily that can wipe out the margin [5].
